beats.narration_text: This week's second video is a general one. Alexandru Gair-gay has an essay called A Lot of Unit Tests Are Worse Than Useless. This is Sai. His example is a book service with five dependencies, all mocked. I ported it to Python and planted bugs in it. The question is his: what does a test like that actually test?

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
the bug and refactor counts land as result lines
the 0% query-code line lands last and holds

props.command: This unit test mocks all five of BookService's dependencies and verifies each one was called once. What behaviour does it actually test, and which bugs would it miss?
props.runningText: planting bugs in a port of the article's example…
output: 5 planted bugs: mocks caught 2, real DB 5
query code: 0% run by the mock tests

beats.narration_text: Here is everything the article's test checks. The validator was called once. The permission check, once. The repository, once. The mapper, once. The metric, once. And the title that comes back is the title it told the mock mapper to return. His point: it mirrors the method's implementation, not its behaviour. The real database never takes part.

show.event: the five verified calls land one by one
the last chip: the title is the one the mock returned
the caption: the article's test, ported

beats.narration_text: So I planted five bugs, one at a time. Three were in the query, his broken assumptions about what would be returned: columns in the wrong order, a raw row instead of a book, an error where not found should be. Two were wiring mistakes in the service. Thirteen mock tests caught the two wiring mistakes, and passed all three query bugs. Four tests against a real database caught all five.

show.event: one planted bug at a time
it splits: the real-database tests and the mock tests
the badges land: 5 of 5, and 2 of 5

data.slideMeta: FIVE BUGS · ONE AT A TIME

tracks.label: real DB, 4 tests
notes: a raw row, not a Book

beats.narration_text: Now the other direction: two changes that keep the behaviour. Move the not-found check into the repository. Build the reply in the service instead of the mapper. The database tests passed both. The mock tests failed both, because they check which calls were made, not what came back. He asks: if a refactor means rewriting the tests, what assurance do they give anymore?

show.event: the fork: which suite survives a behaviour-preserving refactor
mocks fail both; the database tests pass both
the resolver names the two refactors

data.question: Two refactors that change no behaviour: which suite still passes?

branches.label: Real DB, 4 tests
branches.detail: checks the book a caller gets back

resolver.label: It can't guard a refactor it fails
resolver.detail: R1: not-found check moved into the repository · R2: reply built in the service, not the mapper

data.ghostText: both refactors pass the same four database tests, unchanged

beats.narration_text: Coverage won't show this. It asks whether a line ran, and the mock tests run every line of the service: seventeen of seventeen. Mutation testing asks whether a test notices when a line is wrong: change the code one small way at a time, and count the changes that make a test fail. Across thirty-one thousand test suites, once their size was held fixed, coverage was only weakly to moderately tied to catching faults.

show.event: coverage: lines run over lines
the mock tests: 17 of 17 lines of the service, 100%
mutation score: mutants caught over mutants

props.title: Did the line run, or would a test notice?
props.note: coverage.py 7.16 on service.py · mutmut 3.8: a mutant is caught when a test fails
props.conditions: Inozemtseva & Holmes, ICSE 2014: 31,000 suites; low-to-moderate correlation once suite size is held fixed. Just et al., FSE 2014: catching mutants tracks catching real faults.

beats.narration_text: So I ran it on all three test sets. Set aside the mutants that only reword an error message, which no test here checks. Of forty-two left, the mock tests caught thirty-three, and the four database tests forty-one. In the query code, the mocks caught none. Plain unit tests on pure pricing logic caught twenty-eight of thirty. Every mutant the mocks missed sits in that query code, which no mock test runs.

show.event: mocks across the service: 78.6
the real-database tests: 97.6
mocks on the query code: 0
unit tests on pure pricing logic: 93.3

props.title: Behaviour mutants caught, by suite
props.note: Recorded 2026-10-09: evidence/bookservice/mutation_run.py. 33/42, 41/42, 0/9, 28/30. Set aside: 11 that only reword a message, 2 that only change SQL letter case.

beats.narration_text: He is not against unit tests. They shine on pure logic, like his pricing calculator: input in, output out, nothing to mock. The two mutants mine missed point at a real gap, a zero-price item. The trouble is glue: code that moves data through a database you mocked away. Spotify's testing honeycomb, which the essay cites, puts most tests there, at integration.

show.event: a unit test
it splits: pure logic, or glue with mocks
the badges land: 28 of 30, and query code 0 of 9

beats.narration_text: So: one page. A test that mirrors the code can't catch the code being wrong. Here the mock tests ran every line of the service, missed every query bug, and failed both harmless refactors. Four tests against a real database caught what they missed. Unit tests earn their place on pure logic.

show.event: the artifact card opens on the mirror
the bugs, the refactors and the mutation scores fill in
the pure-logic line closes it

props.artifactHeading: Mocks, a real database, one page
artifactLines: A test that mocks every dependency checks the calls the code makes, not what a caller gets back (after Gherghe, 2026).
Of five planted bugs, 13 mock tests caught 2 and passed all three query bugs; 4 tests on a real SQLite database caught all 5.
Mocks failed both behaviour-preserving refactors; the database tests passed both. Mutants caught: 33 of 42 against 41 of 42.
Unit tests on pure pricing logic caught 28 of 30. Coverage is a weak target (Inozemtseva & Holmes, 2014).

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one unit test you trust, with its mocks, and paste this. Ask what each mock assumes about the real thing behind it. Then ask for the smallest bug in that real thing your test would still pass. If there is one, that is where an integration test belongs.

show.event: the handoff prompt types in under 'Your turn.'
the mocks' assumptions stack as it fills
the integration test line lands and the cursor holds

props.command: Here is one of my unit tests and the code it tests. List every assumption its mocks make about the real dependencies. For each, show the smallest bug in that dependency my test would still pass, and the integration test that would catch it.
